# Education in Sweden
The Swedish education system is centered on a nine-year compulsory comprehensive school (grundskola) for children aged 6–16, covering primary and lower secondary education. Preschool education is available from age one, with free access from age three to six hours daily, aiming to support parents’ workforce participation and foundational development through play and pedagogical activities. Compulsory schooling starts with a preschool class at age six and continues through year 9, divided into lower, middle, and upper stages. Students study 16 compulsory subjects including Swedish, mathematics, English, sciences, social studies, arts, and physical education. National tests are administered in grades 3, 6, and 9 for core subjects to ensure uniform assessment.
Upper secondary education (gymnasieskola), lasting three years with nearly 99% enrollment, offers 18 national programs divided into preparatory (academic) and vocational tracks, all providing basic university eligibility while preparatory tracks meet additional requirements for higher education. Admission is competitive and based on grades from compulsory schooling. All upper secondary students must complete a diploma project. After secondary education, students may pursue higher education at universities or university colleges offering Bachelor’s, Master’s, and Doctoral degrees aligned with the Bologna Process. Student aid is managed by the National Board of Student Aid (CSN). Since the 1990s, independent schools (friskolor) have been publicly funded and coexist with state schools, accounting for about 10–15% of enrollments, though their profit-making has drawn political debate. Sweden participates in international academic assessments (PISA, PIRLS), with scores near OECD averages, although immigrant influx and testing inconsistencies have impacted results. The grading system starts in year 6, using A–F marks for passing and failing, supporting transparent progression to upper secondary and higher education.
